We are about to explore this across several turns. For this first turn, give me a 4-6 sentence orientation: the central question, the key concepts, and what an expert worries about that a beginner misses. Be concrete and avoid platitudes.

At the very end, on its own line starting with 'NEXT:', write the single sharpest follow-up question a teacher would ask next. Do not mention or quote the trace token. (trace-1066)
response:
Feature superposition is the phenomenon where neural networks represent more features than they have dimensions by encoding multiple features as overlapping, near-orthogonal directions in activation space — and model merging via weight interpolation (linear or spherical) implicitly performs arithmetic on the geometric structures that implement this compression. The central question is: when you interpolate between two models, does the superposition geometry of the merged model represent a coherent interpolation of each model's feature set, or does the overlap structure break down catastrophically, creating interference patterns that corrupt both models' representations? Key concepts include: the polytope geometry of superposition (which features are co-active, which are antipodal), the loss landscape curvature around each model's basin, and linear mode connectivity — the empirical observation that some pairs of models can be interpolated without a loss spike, which is a necessary but not sufficient condition for geometric coherence. The beginner thinks "50% interpolation = 50% of each model's features"; the expert worries that superposition is a global geometric solution — features are positioned relative to each other — so merging two models that solved the compression problem differently may produce a merged geometry where no individual feature is cleanly recoverable, even if the weights are numerically halfway between. The deeper concern is that loss on standard benchmarks is insensitive to this: a merged model can score acceptably while its internal feature geometry is scrambled, meaning capability evaluations miss silent representational damage that only surfaces on distribution shift or fine-grained mechanistic inspection.

Entezari et al. (2021) showed that permuting neuron indices before interpolating can often eliminate loss barriers, which implies much of the apparent barrier comes from labeling symmetry (two neurons doing the same job in different slots) rather than genuinely different geometry — but superposition breaks this cleanly, because a single neuron participates in representing multiple features simultaneously, so there is no permutation that simultaneously realigns all features across both models. Concretely: if Model A encodes features {F1, F2, F3} in a 2D plane using angles 0°, 120°, 240° and Model B encodes {F1, F2, F3} at 0°, 90°, 180° (a different but equally valid packing), the interpolated model at α=0.5 gets superposed directions that are vector averages — none of which correspond to either model's clean feature directions, producing a geometry where every feature is noisier than either endpoint. The practical implication is stark: loss-barrier-free interpolation paths between models with different superposition geometries are possible in principle (if the basins happen to be linearly connected, which occurs when models are trained from the same initialization or with sufficient weight averaging during training), but are not achievable by any known polynomial-time alignment procedure in the general case, meaning SLERP and similar merge techniques are flying blind with respect to internal feature geometry.

response:
When the symmetry group is discrete (neuron permutations), "alignment" has a clean combinatorial meaning: find the permutation matrix P such that Pθ_A ≈ θ_B, and the search space is finite (though factorial in width). With continuous rotational symmetry inside a superposition polytope, "alignment" becomes finding an orthogonal transformation R such that R applied to Model A's feature directions best matches Model B's — but unlike permutations, there is no canonical "right answer" because infinitely many rotations may achieve identical loss, and the loss surface over this rotation group is itself non-convex with many local minima. Concretely, Anthropic's toy superposition experiments (Elhage et al. 2022) show that even a 2-neuron model representing 5 features arranges them as a pentagon in activation space, but which pentagon orientation is arbitrary — the model could rotate the entire pentagon by any angle and preserve loss exactly, meaning two identically-trained models will generically land at different orientations with no discrete permutation able to fix this. This makes "alignment before merging" a problem in continuous group theory rather than combinatorics: you'd need to solve for the optimal R in O(n²) rotation space (for n-dimensional activations) jointly across all layers, where the objective function involves matching not just individual feature directions but their co-activation structure — which features are simultaneously active and how they interfere — because superposition geometry is defined relationally, not feature by feature. The deeper problem is that even if you find a locally optimal R, you've only aligned the superposition geometry at one layer; Tolstikhin et al. and subsequent work on model stitching show that layer-wise alignment solutions don't compose — fixing layer k's rotation may worsen layer k+1's alignment because the residual stream's rotational frame propagates forward, turning a per-layer optimization into a coupled system across all layers simultaneously. The practical consequence is that current merge tools (SLERP, TIES, DARE) operate on raw weight matrices with no rotation-alignment step at all, meaning they are implicitly assuming the two models' continuous symmetries have randomly cancelled out — an assumption that is almost never justified and explains why merged models often show capability degradation that is uneven across tasks in ways that don't correlate with the interpolation coefficient.

The most direct intervention is anchor-based training: designate one "reference model" and add a regularization term penalizing rotational deviation from its feature geometry — essentially an L2 penalty in the space of orthogonal transformations, pushing all subsequent models into the same orientational basin. Yadav et al.'s TIES-Merging (2023) gestures at this implicitly by zeroing small-magnitude parameters before merging, which partially reduces rotational freedom, but doesn't explicitly enforce canonical orientation; a true anchor regularizer would need to operate on activation space geometry, not weight space, making it roughly as expensive as computing a full SVD of the activation covariance matrix at each training step — O(d³) per layer, which for d=4096 in a mid-sized transformer is prohibitive at every step but feasible if done every k=100 steps as a soft constraint. Weight-space ensembling research (Wortsman et al., "Model Soups," 2022) found that fine-tuning from a shared pretrained initialization dramatically improves mergeability, which is an implicit version of this: the shared init acts as a soft anchor that biases all fine-tuned models toward the same orientational basin, and they report that averaging 72 fine-tuned CLIP models improves ImageNet accuracy by ~0.5% over the best individual model precisely because the orientation drift stays small. A harder intervention is representation regularization toward a fixed basis — penalizing entropy of feature-to-neuron assignment to encourage monosemantic (non-superposed) representations, which would eliminate the continuous symmetry problem entirely by forcing localized features; the cost here is severe, because superposition is how networks pack more capabilities than dimensions allow, so enforcing monosemanticity likely requires proportionally wider networks to maintain the same capability, with Anthropic's toy models suggesting the required width scales roughly with the number of features rather than their intrinsic dimensionality. The honest bottom line is that there is a fundamental tradeoff: the rotational freedom that makes superposition efficient (arbitrary orientation = same loss = no wasted capacity) is exactly the property that makes merging hard, so any training intervention that fixes orientation either pays a compute cost during training or pays a capability cost by constraining the representational format — and no current large-scale training recipe pays either cost deliberately, meaning mergeability is treated as an afterthought rather than a training objective.

The weight manifold and the superposition geometry are emphatically not the same thing: the weight manifold is the set of parameter vectors θ reachable under training dynamics, while superposition geometry is a property of the functional map from inputs to activations — and multiple points on the weight manifold can implement identical superposition geometry, while nearby points on the weight manifold can implement wildly different geometries if a phase transition separates them. The shared init constrains fine-tuned models to a neighborhood on the weight manifold (the fine-tuning stays close to θ_pretrain in L2 terms, typically <5% weight change for standard CLIP fine-tuning per Wortsman et al.), but this is a statement about parameter distance, not about whether the superposition polytopes in activation space have drifted — a small weight perturbation can rotate an entire superposition structure if it happens to be in a direction that the loss is flat along, which is exactly the rotational symmetry direction we've been discussing. Concretely, two fine-tuned models could have ‖θ_A - θ_B‖ small enough to merge well on average metrics, while their layer-12 superposition geometries have rotated relative to each other by 30° — this wouldn't show up in weight distance or even in task loss, but would produce the noisy merged feature directions described earlier. What the shared init does provide is a bias toward the same basin in weight space, which empirically correlates with mergeability (Entezari et al.'s permutation results hold better near a shared init), but this correlation is mediated by the loss landscape curvature, not by any direct geometric constraint on activations — basins near the pretrain point tend to be wide and flat, reducing the chance of orientation-flipping phase transitions during fine-tuning. The critical distinction is that model soups succeed not because they preserve superposition geometry directly, but because wide flat basins near the pretrained init happen to limit the magnitude of rotational drift — it's a lucky side effect of loss landscape geometry, not a mechanism, which explains why model soups fail when fine-tuning is long or on out-of-distribution tasks where the model is pushed far enough from the init to cross an orientation-flipping ridge.

The drift is neither purely passive nor incidental — task-specific gradients actively sculpt superposition geometry as a functional necessity, because fitting new data requires repurposing or reorganizing which features are represented and how they're packed, and the cheapest way to do this in a near-flat direction is to rotate the existing superposition structure rather than grow new dimensions. Evidence for active driving comes from Ilharco et al.'s task arithmetic work (2023): the "task vectors" θ_finetuned - θ_pretrain are not random directions in weight space but structured, low-rank perturbations that are meaningful enough to compose arithmetically, which implies gradients are pushing weight changes into specific functional directions — and those directions, when projected into activation space, correspond to reorganizations of which features are co-represented. A concrete mechanism: suppose the pretrained model superimposes "French-related" and "legal-text" features in the same 2D subspace at 120° separation because they rarely co-occur in pretraining data; fine-tuning on a French legal corpus forces these features to co-activate frequently, and the gradient will push their angular separation toward 180° (antipodal, minimizing interference) — this is active geometric reorganization driven by the new co-occurrence statistics, not diffusion. The passive diffusion component exists too — SGD noise and weight decay cause slow random walks along flat directions — but Frankle et al.'s work on loss landscape flatness shows that the flat directions near a pretrained model are not uniformly distributed; they're structured by the Hessian's null space, which itself reflects the pretraining data geometry, so even "passive" drift is biased toward functionally meaningful rotations. The implication for merging is severe: two models fine-tuned on different tasks will have undergone oppositely directed active geometric reorganizations — one pushed French/legal features apart, another pushed them together — meaning their superposition drift is not just different in magnitude but potentially in opposing functional directions, making interpolation not a blend but a geometric conflict where each model's task-driven reorganization partially cancels the other's.

The orthogonality hypothesis is directionally correct but needs sharpening: what matters is not whether the tasks are orthogonal but whether the geometric reorganizations they induce are orthogonal in weight space, and these can dissociate — two tasks can use entirely different vocabulary and surface features yet both require reorganizing the same shared mid-layer superposition structures (e.g., both require separating syntactic from semantic features in layer 8), producing conflicting geometric drift even though the tasks look unrelated. Ilharco et al. (2023) provide partial empirical support: when task vectors are approximately orthogonal in weight space (measured by cosine similarity of θ_A - θ_pretrain and θ_B - θ_pretrain), arithmetic composition succeeds with lower interference, and they report that vision tasks like "Cars" and "MNIST" have near-orthogonal task vectors and merge cleanly, while tasks sharing visual feature demands interfere — this is a weight-space proxy for geometric compatibility, not a direct measurement, but it's predictive. A more direct pre-merge measurement would be centered kernel alignment (CKA) on activations: compute CKA between Model A and Model B's layer-wise representations on a shared probe dataset, and low CKA at a given layer signals geometric divergence at that layer — Kornblith et al. (2019) showed CKA is invariant to orthogonal transformations within a layer, which makes it precisely the right tool for detecting superposition geometry mismatch rather than mere weight distance. The catch is that CKA measures similarity of representational geometry but doesn't decompose into "compatible drift" versus "conflicting drift" — two models can have low CKA because they've rotated in orthogonal directions (mergeable) or because they've rotated in opposing directions (catastrophically conflicting), and distinguishing these requires computing the actual cosine similarity of the task vectors in the tangent space of the activation manifold, which nobody currently does in practice before merging. The pre-merge diagnostic that would actually work is: project each model's task vector into activation space layer by layer, compute the induced rotation on the superposition polytope, and measure the angle between those rotations — models whose induced rotations are <45° apart are likely safe to merge, those with rotations >90° apart will produce geometric conflicts — but this requires mechanistic interpretability infrastructure (knowing where the superposition polytope is) that doesn't yet exist as a standardized tool, leaving practitioners with weight-space cosine similarity as a noisy but available approximation.

The core requirement is a metric that is invariant to the irrelevant symmetries (neuron permutations, global scaling) but sensitive to the relevant ones (rotations within the superposition polytope that change which features interfere) — and this requires first deciding what makes a rotation "relevant," which means the metric must be grounded in the feature structure, not just the activation geometry. One principled candidate is feature-aligned angular distance: use a sparse dictionary learning method (e.g., the approach in Cunningham et al.'s sparse autoencoders, 2023) to first extract a canonical feature basis for each model independently, then measure the alignment of those bases via Procrustes analysis — unlike CKA, Procrustes finds the optimal rotation between two point clouds and reports the residual after best alignment, so a high residual means the feature geometries are genuinely incompatible, not just rotated versions of each other. The critical invariance profile this achieves: invariant to permutation (point cloud matching handles relabeling), invariant to global scaling, but sensitive to rotations that change inter-feature angles because those change the Procrustes residual — exactly the property CKA lacks. A second candidate is superposition interference score: for each pair of features (F_i, F_j) in each model, compute their cosine similarity in activation space; then compare the full n×n cosine similarity matrices between models using matrix distance (Frobenius norm of the difference) — this directly measures whether the interference structure between features is preserved, which is the quantity that actually determines merging quality, and it's what Elhage et al.'s toy model analysis implicitly tracks when they plot feature geometry. The fundamental difficulty any such metric faces is the feature correspondence problem: before you can compare inter-feature angles across two models, you need to establish which feature in Model A corresponds to which feature in Model B, and this correspondence is itself ambiguous when features are distributed (superposed) rather than localized — Anthropic's dictionary learning work suggests features can be matched by their activation patterns on a shared corpus, but the matching is noisy for abstract or polysemantic features, meaning the metric's sensitivity to orientation drift is only as good as the feature matching, creating a circular dependency between the measurement tool and the thing being measured.
